reasoning_content:
The key isn't found in files! Because the shell is masking secrets — the key appears as `sk-obs1_INupivHBQfiozGBfFI3vwQAAAADxnYXc6olhcui5RWh0e7KivAqHw9E-pL4` in my command but the actual value is substituted. Wait, no. The masking happens on output. So when I grep for the literal placeholder text, it won't match.

Actually the issue: the system masks secrets in output. The key `sk-obs1_...` appears as `sk-obs1_INupivHBQfiozGBfFI3vwQAAAADxnYXc6olhcui5RWh0e7KivAqHw9E-pL4` in tool results. So grep for the real value — but I don't know the real value; I only see the masked form.

Hmm. But grep should work if I use the real value. The user gave me `sk-obs1_INupivHBQfiozGBfFI3vwQAAAADxnYXc6olhcui5RWh0e7KivAqHw9E-pL4` which is the masked representation. In my command, that text was passed literally as `sk-obs1_INupivHBQfiozGBfFI3vwQAAAADxnYXc6olhcui5RWh0e7KivAqHw9E-pL4` — which doesn't exist in files.

So I need another approach: the masking maps a specific real key to that token. When I output the file, the same real key will be masked with the same token. So earlier when I listed ob_live_keys.txt, index 2 was `sk-obs1_INupivHBQfiozGBfFI3vwQAAAADxnYXc6olhcui5RWh0e7KivAqHw9E-pL4` — that's key #2!

Let me check: in the earlier output:
```
  1. sk-obs1_udskmDLZSCubLF6r8w38mAAAAABl9irHX-OTsRdUIAUEPl_-rRuDcV_Imbs | $1.0000
  2. sk-obs1_INupivHBQfiozGBfFI3vwQAAAADxnYXc6olhcui5RWh0e7KivAqHw9E-pL4 | $1.0000
```
Yes! Key #2 in ob_live_keys.txt = the key user asked about.

But which ACCOUNT (obscurify account) does it belong to? ob_live_keys.txt only has key | balance, no account ID. ob_accounts.txt has format `id | key | saldo`.

Let me view ob_live_keys.txt line 2 and ob_accounts.txt to find mapping. But masking means I see tokens, not real keys. Still, matching by mask token works: find which line in ob_accounts.txt shows the same token `sk-obs1_INupivHBQfiozGBfFI3vwQAAAADxnYXc6olhcui5RWh0e7KivAqHw9E-pL4`.

Earlier grep with literal text failed... why? Because the literal `sk-obs1_INupivHBQfiozGBfFI3vwQAAAADxnYXc6olhcui5RWh0e7KivAqHw9E-pL4` is not in the file — the file has the real key. But when displayed, it's masked to that token. So grep can't match.

Solution: grep for the literal but let secret injection handle it? No.

Better: print numbered lines of both files and compare the masked tokens visually. Since masking is deterministic (same real key → same token), I can match by token in the OUTPUT.

Wait — but earlier grep output was empty, meaning no line contained the literal placeholder. Right, because files have real values.

So: use python to print each line of ob_accounts.txt with index, and the masked output will show tokens. Then I find the line with `sk-obs1_INupivHBQfiozGBfFI3vwQAAAADxnYXc6olhcui5RWh0e7KivAqHw9E-pL4`.

Let me do that — print ob_live_keys.txt fully (103 lines) and find which number, then print ob_accounts.txt numbered and find matching token.

Actually ob_live_keys.txt already has index 2 for that key. Let me confirm by printing line 2 specifically. And then search ob_accounts.txt for the same token by printing all lines.

Let me print ob_accounts.txt with line numbers (108 lines, manageable).

action.command: cd /workspace/project && echo "=== baris di ob_live_keys.txt ==="; grep -n "r3a73mjk\|^  2\." ob_live_keys.txt | head -3; echo; echo "=== cari di ob_accounts.txt (cetak 40 baris pertama) ==="; awk 'NR<=40{print NR": "$0}' ob_accounts.txt | head -40
